subtype: Reading a speaker's gestures for meaning [Interpreting]
passage: Madhav Sir stood in the schoolyard with a bucket of water beside the dry drain. “Last monsoon the water in the well rose this high,” he said, sweeping his hand up above his head. Darshan's eyes followed the hand. That was taller than he was! But Sir's arm was stretched wide in the way he always tells stories. Darshan raised his hand. “Sir, is that really how high it was?” Sir laughed. “Good question. My hand was showing the mood. It was really up to here,” and he tapped his waist.

qa.q: What was next to the dry drain?
qa.a: A bucket of water was beside the dry drain.

qa.q: What was Darshan thinking when he asked if that was really how high the water had been?
qa.a: He wanted to check the meaning, since the gesture looked bigger than he expected and he knew Sir stretches his arm when telling stories. He may also have been a little worried he was misunderstanding.

qa.q: What would help pupils read a teacher's gestures for meaning?
qa.a: Watch the gesture and the words together, and ask a follow-up question, as Darshan did, when the picture seems exaggerated.

qa.q: How might Madhav Sir see his own gesture?
qa.a: As a lively way to make the story vivid, without realising it could mislead. He was pleased Darshan asked.

grounding: A pupil reads a teacher's hand gestures for size and checks the meaning by asking.

subtype: Reading a speaker's gestures for meaning [Interpreting]
passage: In the science room in Istanbul, Pablo swept one hand in a wide curve above the desk. “The moon goes around the Earth like this,” he said. Zeynep watched the hand. It seemed to make a huge loop, then dip low, then rise. “Does the moon go up and down like a roller coaster?” she asked. Pablo laughed. “No, my hand wobbled. Thanks for asking.” He drew a circle on the board with the Earth in the middle. “Here. A steady round path.” Zeynep nodded. “Oh. It's more like a circle.”

qa.q: Where did the science lesson take place?
qa.a: It took place in the science room in Istanbul.

qa.q: What was Zeynep thinking when she asked if the moon goes up and down?
qa.a: She was trying to understand what she saw in his hand movement, which looked like a wobbly loop. She might have been a little unsure but willing to ask.

qa.q: What could Zeynep do when a gesture seems unclear?
qa.a: Ask a follow-up question, as she did, so the teacher can explain or draw it.

qa.q: What would change if Pablo had only used gestures and no board?
qa.a: Pupils might keep the wobbly picture of the moon's path, since gestures can clarify but also mislead. The drawing corrected it.

grounding: A pupil watches a teacher's hands describing a path and checks the meaning with a question.

subtype: Reading a speaker's gestures for meaning [Interpreting]
passage: In the science lab, Rukmini Ma'am was explaining how a ball rolls down a ramp. Her right hand swooped down steeply, then shot along the bench. “It speeds up like this!” Tanvir watched her hand. So it goes really fast at the bottom, faster than a cycle? When they tried it, the marble trundled down and rolled gently off the end. Tanvir frowned and raised his hand. “Ma'am, your hand went way faster than the marble. Which is right?” Ma'am laughed. “Good catch. My hands exaggerate. It does speed up, but only a little on a ramp this small. Let's time it and see.”

qa.q: What did the marble do at the end of the ramp?
qa.a: The marble rolled gently off the end.

qa.q: What was Tanvir feeling when the marble rolled gently?
qa.a: Tanvir felt puzzled, because the gesture had made him expect something much faster.

qa.q: Why was Tanvir's follow-up question useful?
qa.a: It checked the gesture against what he saw, and led Ma'am to admit her hands exaggerated and to time it properly.

qa.q: How did Rukmini Ma'am react to being corrected?
qa.a: She laughed, called it a good catch and turned it into a timing test, so she was glad he asked.

grounding: Shows a pupil reading a teacher's gestures for speed in a demo, noticing they exaggerated, and asking to check.

subtype: Reading a speaker's gestures for meaning [Interpreting]
passage: I'm Gurleen, and Deepika sits in front of me in geography. Sir was describing how the river flows from the mountains. He held his left hand high for the mountain, then waved his right hand down and away to his right. Deepika drew the path in her notebook, arrow going right. But on the wall map the river flows left, towards the sea. Sir was facing us, so his right was our left. Deepika looked from her notebook to the map and back, frowning. Then she put her hand up. “Sir, is it flowing left or right?” He looked at his own hand and laughed. “Left, from where you sit. My hands were backwards for you.”

qa.q: Which way does the river flow on the wall map?
qa.a: On the wall map the river flows left, towards the sea.

qa.q: What was Deepika feeling when she looked from her notebook to the map?
qa.a: She was confused and a little unsure, because the gesture and the map didn't match.

qa.q: What did Deepika's question achieve?
qa.a: It showed the teacher's gesture was mirrored from the class's side, so everyone could correct their arrows.

qa.q: How did Gurleen make sense of the mix-up?
qa.a: Gurleen worked out that Sir was facing the class, so his right was their left.

grounding: Shows a pupil following a teacher's direction gestures, being misled by a mirrored picture, and asking to check the meaning.

subtype: Reading a speaker's gestures for meaning [Interpreting]
passage: Tuesday: Suraj Bhaiya was teaching Sunaina to bowl in the lane. “Land it here,” he said, and his hand dipped to the ground, then bounced up to his knee. Sunaina bowled. The ball smacked into the ground halfway and bounced over his head. Thursday: She tried again, watching his hands closely. His hand bounced to his knee again, but he was crouching this time, so his knee was lower. She bowled even shorter. Saturday: Before bowling, Sunaina asked, “Bhaiya, show me with something real where it lands. Your hands keep changing.” He drew a chalk mark on the lane. Her next ball hit it.

qa.q: What did Suraj draw on the lane on Saturday?
qa.a: He drew a chalk mark on the lane.

qa.q: What was Sunaina feeling by Saturday?
qa.a: Sunaina was frustrated and confused by the changing hand signs, and determined to get a clearer answer.

qa.q: Why did asking for a real mark work better?
qa.a: A chalk mark showed exactly where to land the ball, while his hand gestures kept changing and misled her.

qa.q: How might Suraj see his hand gestures after Saturday?
qa.a: Suraj might realise his gestures weren't as clear as he thought, and that a real mark helps more.

grounding: Shows a child reading a speaker's hand gestures for height and distance, being misled, and asking a follow-up to check.

subtype: Reading a speaker's gestures for meaning [Interpreting]
passage: "Amandeep, you watch your science teacher's hands closely. Good. I, your Gautam Tauji, learned that the hard way. Our teacher in Class 6, Mr Bhatt, loved big gestures. One day he talked about dropping a stone and a feather. For the stone, his hand shot down like lightning. For the feather, his fingers floated side to side, slow as a leaf. So I wrote in my notebook: heavy things always fall faster. Something bothered me, though, and after class I asked, 'Sir, would a heavy stone and a small stone land together?' He stopped, then laughed. 'Yes! My hands made the feather too dramatic. It's the air that slows it.' Always ask, beta."

qa.q: What did young Gautam write in his notebook?
qa.a: Heavy things always fall faster.

qa.q: What was young Gautam feeling when something bothered him after class?
qa.a: Doubtful and curious, uneasy that the idea he got from the gestures might be wrong, which pushed him to ask.

qa.q: What choice in the story fixed the mistaken idea?
qa.a: Gautam's follow-up question, whether a heavy and a small stone would land together, made the teacher explain that it is the air that slows the feather.

qa.q: How did Mr Bhatt react to the question?
qa.a: He stopped, laughed and admitted his hands had made the feather too dramatic; he seems glad the question caught the mistake.

grounding: It is an elder's memory of a teacher's exaggerated gestures giving a wrong idea about falling objects, and a follow-up question checking the meaning.
